differences.title: 1. THREAT MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Kata Containers runs each pod in a lightweight VM to reduce kernel-sharing risk, but it still integrates closely with the container runtime stack and relies on a Linux guest kernel boundary as the primary isolation primitive.
differences.rightDesc: Firecracker is built around a strong microVM boundary for workloads that can’t trust the host kernel. It minimizes exposed devices and surfaces fewer kernel-level attack paths than traditional containers.

differences.title: 2. INTEGRATION SURFACE
differences.leftDesc: Kata Containers integrates with container orchestration via runtime shims (e.g., containerd/CRI-O) so Kubernetes can treat pods like containers while internally launching a VM per pod or sandbox, coordinating cgroups, mounts, and networking.
differences.rightDesc: Firecracker is typically orchestrated by higher-level tooling that provisions microVMs via its API, using a minimal device model. Your platform is responsible for mapping workloads to microVM lifecycles.

differences.title: 3. BOOT & STARTUP LATENCY
differences.leftDesc: Kata’s sandbox VM startup depends on VM image, guest kernel, and the init path inside the guest. It typically performs best when VMs are reused or pre-warmed by orchestration strategies.
differences.rightDesc: Firecracker is optimized for short-lived workloads: it uses a minimal initramfs/boot flow, tight device emulation, and reduced configuration. This keeps time-to-ready low for bursty request patterns.

differences.title: 4. DEVICE EMULATION
differences.leftDesc: Kata’s guest environment aims for broad Linux container compatibility, supporting common paravirt devices and integration patterns so existing container images behave similarly inside the guest VM.
differences.rightDesc: Firecracker intentionally implements only the essential virtual devices (e.g., virtio-net/virtio-block) and avoids legacy emulation. Fewer virtual devices mean less complexity and smaller attack surface.

differences.title: 5. RESOURCE ACCOUNTING
differences.leftDesc: Kata maps pod/container resource limits to host mechanisms (like cgroups) and ensures CPU/memory and IO constraints apply to the VM sandbox, so quotas defined at the orchestration layer remain enforceable.
differences.rightDesc: Firecracker runs a microVM whose CPU/memory are constrained by the host (commonly via cgroups). The platform controlling microVM creation must enforce sizing and limits per tenant/workload.

differences.title: 6. NETWORKING MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Kata is designed to work smoothly with Kubernetes networking (CNI) by presenting pod-level network semantics while the workload runs inside the VM. IP, routes, and DNS are managed like standard pods.
differences.rightDesc: Firecracker’s networking is typically implemented using virtio-net in the guest, connected to host-side networking constructs. You compose VPC/CNI-like behavior outside Firecracker based on your platform.

differences.title: 7. OPERATIONAL OPTIMIZATION
differences.leftDesc: Kata relies on orchestration-aware management for VM lifecycle, often benefiting from sandbox reuse patterns at the pod level. Operational tuning focuses on image management, guest kernel selection, and node-level performance.
differences.rightDesc: With Firecracker, operators typically focus on microVM pooling/reuse, image caching, and placement to reduce repeated boot costs. Because Firecracker is lower-level, platform tooling heavily influences operational efficiency.
